paragraphes: One morning, the power goes out at your whole school. No lights, no computers, no bell.
Lessons go on in the yard, with paper and pencils. At the same time, workers fix the power.
Two things happen together. Some people keep the important work going. Others repair the damage. A company plans for both. The two plans are called business continuity and disaster recovery.

decouverte.comme: One team keeps teaching in spite of the power cut. Another team fixes the power to get back to normal.
decouverte.enVrai: Business continuity (BC) keeps the most important work running during a crisis. Disaster recovery (DR) puts the computer systems back to normal. A disaster is a big event that stops the work, like a fire. The image stops here: a company makes these plans before the crisis, not during it.

decouverte.question: Ransomware is a program that locks your files until you pay. It locks all the computers of an online shop. Which plan should the shop start?
options: Only the recovery plan
Only the continuity plan
Both plans, at the same time
decouverte.answer: Both plans, at the same time
decouverte.explanation: The manual says that both start together. One keeps the main work going. The other fixes the systems. Each other answer forgets half of the job.

decouverte.titre: A hospital and its computer failure
decouverte.texte: The patient files cannot be opened. The nurses switch to paper files. This is continuity, because care does not stop. At the same time, the IT team makes the system work again. This is recovery.

cards.question: Official definition: “business continuity plan (BCP)”
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: In simple words: a plan, with written steps, that keeps the most important work going during a crisis. COOP is another name for it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “business continuity plan (BCP)”?
options: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to restore their key business functions after the end of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).

A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).

A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep all of their business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).

A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as disaster recovery (DR).
options_why: This is about recovery after the crisis. A continuity plan keeps the work running during the crisis.
It says all functions. The real sentence says key functions.
COOP means continuity of operations. It is another name for the BCP, not for DR.
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: keep, key business functions, in the event of a crisis.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “business continuity plan (BCP)” from memory.
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: Three parts: a written method, keep the key functions running, and in the event of a crisis.

cards.question: Official definition: “disaster recovery plan (DRP)”
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the steps to fix the systems and the work after something bad stops them. It must be done in a safe and quick way.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “disaster recovery plan (DRP)”?
options: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with keeping your key business functions running, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, quickly and cheaply, after a disruptive event occurs.
A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, before a disruptive event occurs.
A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
options_why: This describes continuity. Recovery is about restoring the systems.
The real words are securely and efficiently. Cheap is not in the sentence.
Recovery starts after the event. It does not start before it.
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: restoring, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “disaster recovery plan (DRP)” from memory.
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: Remember the two words: securely and efficiently. They mean in a safe way and in a smart way.

cards.question: Official definition: “DR compared with BC”
cards.answer: DR is the subset of BC whose primary objective is to minimize business downtime and reclaim normal operations as soon as possible.
cards.explanation: In simple words: recovery is one part of continuity. It is the part that brings everything back to normal fast.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. A subset is a smaller part of a bigger group.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “DR compared with BC” from memory.
cards.answer: DR is the subset of BC whose primary objective is to minimize business downtime and reclaim normal operations as soon as possible.
cards.explanation: Three parts: a subset of BC, minimize downtime, and get back to normal as soon as possible.

cards.question: A fire destroys a company's office. Which action is part of disaster recovery (DR)?
options: Repairing the destroyed computer systems and data
Moving the staff to a temporary office
Telling customers that orders now go by phone
Sending goods from another warehouse
options_why: This lets people work during the crisis. That is continuity.
This keeps sales going during the crisis. That is continuity.
This keeps the key part of the business running. That is continuity.
cards.answer: Repairing the destroyed computer systems and data
cards.explanation: Recovery puts the systems and the data back in order.

cards.question: Which plan keeps the key business functions running during a crisis?
options: The disaster recovery plan (DRP)
A backup of all the files
The business continuity plan (BCP)
A list of all the company computers
options_why: The DRP restores the systems after the event. It does not keep the whole business running.
A backup helps to get data back. It is not a plan for the whole business.
A list helps to know what you own, but it does not keep any work going.
cards.answer: The business continuity plan (BCP)
cards.explanation: Continuity is about keeping the essential work going while the crisis lasts.

cards.question: Which plan is broad and covers all the key functions of a company, not only IT?
options: The disaster recovery plan (DRP)
A plan for one single computer system
A plan that only lists staff phone numbers
The business continuity plan (BCP)
options_why: The DRP is narrower. It focuses on systems, applications, and data.
One system is too small. The BCP covers the whole company.
Phone numbers can be a part of the plan, but they are not the whole plan.
cards.answer: The business continuity plan (BCP)
cards.explanation: The BCP is broad: all critical business functions. The DRP is narrower.

cards.question: What does COOP stand for?
cards.answer: Continuity of operations. It is another name for the business continuity plan (BCP).
cards.explanation: Two names for one idea: keeping the operations running.

cards.question: A flood stops the main office of a company. When is the BEST time to start continuity and recovery work?
options: Recovery first, and continuity only when the systems work again
At the same time, right after the event
Continuity first, and recovery only after one week
Only after management writes a final report
options_why: Waiting to restart the key work would stop the business for too long.
A week is too long. The systems must be repaired from the start.
A report is useful later, but the work must start right away.
cards.answer: At the same time, right after the event
cards.explanation: The manual says that BC and DR start together. One keeps the work going, the other repairs.

cards.question: Which statement about BC and DR is MOST correct?
options: BC is one part of DR that fixes the servers
BC and DR are two names for the same plan
DR is a part of BC that restores normal work quickly
DR keeps the work going and BC repairs the systems
options_why: It is the other way round. DR is the smaller part.
They work together, but they are not the same plan.
These roles are swapped. BC keeps the work going and DR repairs.
cards.answer: DR is a part of BC that restores normal work quickly
cards.explanation: The manual says that DR is a subset of BC. A subset is a smaller part.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT part of disaster recovery?
options: Letting staff work from home
Restoring a server from a backup
Repairing a destroyed network
Reinstalling lost applications
options_why: Restoring a server is exactly what recovery does.
Repairing the network puts the technology back in order. That is recovery.
Reinstalling applications puts the systems back in order. That is recovery.
cards.answer: Letting staff work from home
cards.explanation: Working from home keeps the business running. That is continuity, not recovery.

cards.question: What is the difference between BC and DR? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: BC keeps the key work running during the crisis. DR brings the systems back to normal after the event.
cards.explanation: Think of the school: teachers keep teaching, workers fix the power.

cards.question: A data center is a big room full of servers. Which crisis can a business continuity plan cover?
options: Only a flood that shuts down the whole data center
A ransomware attack or a data center shut by a flood
Only an attack by hackers on the network
Only the failure of one worker's laptop
options_why: Attacks are covered too. The plan covers all critical crises.
Natural disasters are covered too. The plan is not only about attacks.
A laptop is too small. The plan covers crises that hit key functions.
cards.answer: A ransomware attack or a data center shut by a flood
cards.explanation: The manual says that the BCP covers everything, from DDoS and ransomware attacks to natural disasters.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note after the definition of the DRP.

cards.question: On what does the disaster recovery plan focus?
options: Every critical business function
Only the staff and their safety
Only the customers and their orders
Systems, applications, and data
options_why: That is the wide view of the BCP. The DRP is narrower.
People matter, but the DRP is about the technology.
Customers matter, but the DRP is about the technology and the data.
cards.answer: Systems, applications, and data
cards.explanation: Recovery mostly aims at the technology: the systems, the applications, and the data.

cards.question: A hospital loses its computer system. The nurses switch to paper files. Which statement BEST describes this?
options: It is business continuity, because care keeps going
It is disaster recovery, because the nurses fix the problem
It is a failure, because paper is not allowed in a hospital
It is not part of any plan, because it is only a quick fix
options_why: Fixing the system is the job of recovery. Paper files only keep care going.
Paper is a normal backup way of working. It is part of a good plan.
A planned way to keep working is exactly what a continuity plan lists.
cards.answer: It is business continuity, because care keeps going
cards.explanation: Paper files keep the key work going during the crisis. That is continuity.

cards.question: Name two crises that a continuity plan can cover.
cards.answer: Attacks such as ransomware or DDoS (an attack from many computers at once that blocks a service). Also natural disasters that shut down a data center.
cards.explanation: The plan covers all crises, from a computer attack to a natural disaster.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note after the definition of the DRP.

cards.question: Why does a company need both a continuity plan and a recovery plan? Which reason is BEST?
options: Continuity is cheaper, so it can replace recovery
Recovery is needed only when continuity fails to work
Recovery takes time, so continuity keeps work going meanwhile
Both plans do the same job, so one is a spare
options_why: Continuity does not repair anything. The systems still need recovery.
Both start together. Recovery is not a second choice.
The two plans have different jobs. One keeps going, the other repairs.
cards.answer: Recovery takes time, so continuity keeps work going meanwhile
cards.explanation: The repair takes time. The business cannot stop during that time.

cards.question: When do BC and DR start during a disaster?
cards.answer: At the same time. BC keeps the essential work going while DR works to get back to normal.
cards.explanation: Neither one waits for the other.

decouverte.titre: The truck that is too small
paragraphes: You are moving to a new home. Your truck is small. Not everything fits in the first trip.
You choose what goes first: the bed and the fridge. The boxes of decorations can wait. For each object you ask: what happens if I do not have it tonight?
A company does the same thing before a crisis. This work is called a business impact analysis (BIA).

decouverte.comme: For each object, you note how much you need it. Without the bed, you sleep badly. Without the decoration boxes, nobody notices.
decouverte.enVrai: The company lists its critical business functions (CBF). These are the jobs that the business cannot live without. For each one, it asks what a stop would cost. Then it decides what to protect first. The image stops here: in a company, several people decide together.

decouverte.question: Who should help to find the critical functions of a company?
options: Only the IT team
A group: system owners, experts, customers, and suppliers
Only the director
decouverte.answer: A group: system owners, experts, customers, and suppliers
decouverte.explanation: Each person sees the company from a different angle. The IT team does not see everything, and neither does the director.

decouverte.texte: A pizzeria lists what it needs. The cooks are its staff. Taking orders is a process, which means a way of working. The cash register software is a system. The oven is another asset, which means a thing of value. Without the oven there are no pizzas, so it is critical. The monthly newsletter is not.

cards.question: Official definition: “business impact analysis (BIA)”
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: In simple words: the BIA studies what happens to the company, hour after hour, when something stops its work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Business Impact Analysis”. You will need to know this sentence word for word. The ISO is the International Organization for Standardization.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “business impact analysis (BIA)”?
options: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the cause of a disruption on the organization."
According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of reducing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the information systems."
According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
options_why: A BIA looks at the impact over time. It does not look for the cause.
A BIA analyzes the impact. Reducing it is the job of the plans.
The impact is on the whole organization, not only on the systems.
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: process of analyzing, impact over time, disruption.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “business impact analysis (BIA)” from memory.
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: Three parts: a process of analyzing, the impact over time, of a disruption on the organization.

cards.question: Official definition: “what the BIA is for”
cards.answer: In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the BIA finds the key jobs of the company and shows what a disaster would cost each one. It is the main reason for the continuity plan.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Business Impact Analysis”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “what the BIA is for”?
options: In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the final approval for the business continuity plan and its requirements.

In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.

In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and repair the damage that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.

In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the disaster recovery tests and their results.
options_why: The BIA gives the main reason for the plan. It does not approve it.
A BIA studies the impact before a disaster. It does not repair damage.
The BIA justifies the continuity plan, not the recovery tests.
cards.answer: In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: identify its essential business functions, understand the impact, primary justification.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “what the BIA is for” from memory.
cards.answer: In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.
cards.explanation: Two jobs: find the essential functions and their impact, then justify the plan.

cards.question: Which question does a BIA ask about each function of a company?
options: Who built the system that runs this function?
How much did this function cost last year?
What happens if this function stops?
Which worker is the best at this function?
options_why: The builder of a system does not tell what a stop would cost.
Cost is useful, but the BIA looks at the impact of a stop.
Skills are useful, but the BIA looks at the impact on the business.
cards.answer: What happens if this function stops?
cards.explanation: A BIA studies the impact of a stop on the organization, over time.

cards.question: What is a critical business function (CBF)?
options: A job without which the business is really in danger
A job that earns the most money for the company
A job that only the IT team knows how to use
A job that was very hard to build and to test
options_why: Critical does not mean most profitable. A job can be vital and earn little.
A CBF can be anywhere in the business, not only in IT.
Difficulty does not make a function critical. The risk to the business does.
cards.answer: A job without which the business is really in danger
cards.explanation: The key word is business: we look for what is vital for the activity of the company.

cards.question: Which item is a business process, which means a way of working?
options: The payroll software
Taking orders by phone
The delivery truck
The nurses of a hospital
options_why: Software is a system, not a way of working.
A truck is another asset, which means a thing of value.
Nurses are personnel, which means people.
cards.answer: Taking orders by phone
cards.explanation: The manual lists four families: personnel, business processes, information systems and applications, and other assets.

cards.question: What does CBF stand for?
cards.answer: Critical business function: a job that the business cannot live without.
cards.explanation: The key word is business.

cards.question: A company has just listed its critical functions. What is the BEST next step for each one?
options: Buy new equipment for each one
Remove the ones that earn the least money
Hire extra staff for each one
Look for weak points and risks
options_why: We buy nothing before we know what is really in danger.
Critical does not mean profitable. A vital function can earn little.
Hiring does not help while we do not know the weak points.
cards.answer: Look for weak points and risks
cards.explanation: The manual asks for a risk analysis of each function. It looks at weak points, the chance of a problem, and the impact the business accepts.

cards.question: A manager starts a BIA. What should happen FIRST?
options: Form the team and set the scope and budget
Analyze the weak points and risks of each function
Buy backup equipment
Write the recovery steps
options_why: We cannot analyze before we know who works on it and how far it goes.
We do not buy anything before we know what to protect.
Recovery steps come later, after the analysis.
cards.answer: Form the team and set the scope and budget
cards.explanation: The manual says to begin by setting the team, the scope, and the budget.

cards.question: The team, the scope, the budget, and the support of leaders are ready. Which step comes AFTER them?
options: Analyze the acceptable impact of each function
Test the continuity plan
Identify the critical business functions
Close the project
options_why: This is later. We must first know which functions exist.
There is no plan to test yet.
The work has hardly started.
cards.answer: Identify the critical business functions
cards.explanation: Next comes the list of critical functions. Then each one gets a risk analysis.

cards.question: Name one family of critical functions and give an example.
cards.answer: For example: personnel (nurses), processes (taking orders), systems (payroll software), or other assets (a delivery truck).
cards.explanation: The manual lists four families.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: personnel, business processes, information systems and applications, other assets.

cards.question: Who should help to find the critical functions? Which group is MOST complete?
options: The IT team, the director, and the finance team
Only the director and the senior managers of the company
Only the IT team and the system vendors
System owners, experts, customers, and suppliers
options_why: This group sees the inside of the company only. It misses customers and suppliers.
Senior managers see a lot, but they miss customers and suppliers.
Vendors know the systems, but not every business function.
cards.answer: System owners, experts, customers, and suppliers
cards.explanation: Each person sees the company from a different angle. Many points of view give a better list.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Business Impact Analysis”.

cards.question: Why does a continuity plan need the support of senior leaders?
options: It is a legal rule that the leaders of the company must sign each year
It gives no quick return, so it needs money and staff
Only leaders know how to write technical plans
Leaders must run every recovery test themselves
options_why: The manual gives another reason: money, staff, and a strategic view.
Writing the plan is a team job, not a leaders-only job.
Leaders support the plan. They do not run every test.
cards.answer: It gives no quick return, so it needs money and staff
cards.explanation: A danger that has not happened yet brings no profit. Leaders must pay for it anyway.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: BCP does not yield an immediate or tangible return.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four families of critical functions?
options: Personnel, which means the people
Business processes, the ways of working
Competitor strategies and plans
Other assets, the things of value
options_why: People are a family of critical functions.
Ways of working are a family of critical functions.
Things of value are a family of critical functions.
cards.answer: Competitor strategies and plans
cards.explanation: The four families are personnel, business processes, information systems and applications, and other assets.

cards.question: Why is the BIA the main reason for the continuity plan?
cards.answer: It shows which functions matter and what a disaster would cost them. The plan is built from that.
cards.explanation: No BIA means no clear reason for what the plan protects.

cards.question: A company skips the BIA and protects every function in the same way. What is the MOST likely result?
options: Too much money goes to minor functions, too little to vital ones
Every function is protected very well, and the cost stays low for the company
The company no longer needs a continuity plan because it protects everything
The vital functions get double protection by luck, and the rest get none
options_why: Money is limited. Protecting everything the same way wastes it.
The BIA is the reason for the plan. Skipping it does not remove the need.
Without priorities, nothing gives extra care to the vital functions.
cards.answer: Too much money goes to minor functions, too little to vital ones
cards.explanation: The BIA helps to choose. We protect first what hurts most if we lose it.

cards.question: What does a BIA show about the functions of a company?
cards.answer: Which ones are strong and which ones are fragile when something stops the work.
cards.explanation: Resilient means strong when facing a problem.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: a BIA helps to find the more resilient and the more fragile functions.

paragraphes: You play online with three friends. In the middle of the game, your console crashes. The screen goes black.
Your friends wait a little. After ten minutes it feels long. After an hour, they start a new game and stop inviting you.
So there is a longest waiting time. After it, the damage stays. In a company, this limit is called the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD). Downtime means the time when work is stopped.

decouverte.comme: For a while, your friends are ready to wait. Then comes a moment when they leave for good.
decouverte.enVrai: A critical business function (CBF) can stop for a short time without much harm. After the limit, the damage lasts: customers leave and the company is in danger. This limit is the MTD. The image stops here: the person responsible for the function, the system owner, sets the limit.

decouverte.question: An online shop is down. What does its MTD show?
options: The time the technicians expect the repair to take
The longest time the shop can be down before lasting harm
The length of the last failure
decouverte.answer: The longest time the shop can be down before lasting harm
decouverte.explanation: The expected repair time is another measure, which you will see in the next planet. The MTD is a limit, not a forecast.

decouverte.texte: A bakery loses its cash register at seven in the morning. Customers wait a little, then go to the shop next door. If the register stays broken for more than two days, many customers never come back. These two days are the MTD of this function. This is an invented example.

cards.question: Official definition: “maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)”
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the longest time a key function can stay stopped. After that, the harm lasts and the company may not survive.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)”?
options: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the average time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.

Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.

Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing any harm at all to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.

Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's yearly budget.
options_why: The MTD is the longest time. It is not the average.
Some stop is accepted. The harm to avoid is the significant, long-term harm.
The limit is about the survival of the organization, not its budget.
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: total length of time, without significant, long-term harm, the longest time, long-term survival.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)” from memory.
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: It is a long sentence. Remember two halves: before the semicolon and after it.

cards.question: Official definition: “who defines the MTD”
cards.answer: MTD must be defined by the system owner, who is ultimately responsible to the organization for the proper operation of the CBF.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the person who answers for the function decides how long it can stay stopped.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “who defines the MTD” from memory.
cards.answer: MTD must be defined by the system owner, who is ultimately responsible to the organization for the proper operation of the CBF.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the system owner, responsible to the organization, for the proper operation of the CBF.

cards.question: Official definition: “exceeding the MTD”
cards.answer: Exceeding the MTD is an expression of unacceptable risk by the business owner.
cards.explanation: In simple words: going past the MTD means a risk that is too high for the owner.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “exceeding the MTD” from memory.
cards.answer: Exceeding the MTD is an expression of unacceptable risk by the business owner.
cards.explanation: Three parts: exceeding the MTD, unacceptable risk, the business owner.

cards.question: An online shop can be down for two days. After that, many customers leave for good. What do these two days show?
options: The normal length of a repair
The time between two backups
The time needed to warn the customers
Its maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) limit
options_why: A repair lasts as long as it lasts. Here we talk about a limit that must not be passed.
Backups are about lost data, not about the length of the stop.
Warning customers is one action of a plan. It is not the limit before lasting harm.
cards.answer: Its maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) limit
cards.explanation: The two days are the limit before lasting harm. This is exactly the MTD.

cards.question: What does the MTD measure?
options: The longest stop before lasting harm
The data that a company can accept to lose
The usual time needed to repair a system
The money lost in one hour of downtime
options_why: That is a different measure, about data. You will meet it soon.
A usual repair time is a forecast. The MTD is a limit.
Money lost is a cost. The MTD is a length of time.
cards.answer: The longest stop before lasting harm
cards.explanation: The MTD is about time and survival: how long the function can stay stopped.

cards.question: Which name is another name for the MTD?
options: MTO: minimum time online
BCP: business continuity plan
MAO: maximum acceptable outage
COOP: the continuity of operations plan
options_why: This name does not exist in the manual.
The BCP is a plan, not a time limit.
COOP is another name for the BCP, not for the MTD.
cards.answer: MAO: maximum acceptable outage
cards.explanation: Two names for the same limit: MTD or MAO.

cards.question: What is the other name of the MTD?
cards.answer: MAO: maximum acceptable outage.
cards.explanation: An outage is a time when a service does not work.

cards.question: Technicians say that a shop can be down for 10 hours. The system owner says that customers leave after 3 hours. Which value should the company use as the MTD?
options: 10 hours, because technicians know the system best
6.5 hours, the average of both
13 hours, both numbers added
3 hours, because the owner sets it
options_why: Technicians know the repair, but the owner knows what a stop costs the business.
An average is not a limit. The MTD comes from the owner.
Adding the numbers has no meaning for the MTD.
cards.answer: 3 hours, because the owner sets it
cards.explanation: The system owner answers for the function, so the owner defines the MTD.

cards.question: The MTD of an important function is not known. What should the company do FIRST?
options: Buy faster servers to be safe
Ask the system owner what stop the business can bear
Use the repair time that the IT team prefers
Copy the MTD of another company
options_why: We cannot choose a solution before we know the limit.
The IT team knows the repair, not the cost of a stop.
Another company has other customers and other risks.
cards.answer: Ask the system owner what stop the business can bear
cards.explanation: The owner knows what a long stop would cost. The limit starts from the business.

cards.question: Which statement about the MTD is MOST correct?
options: It is a forecast of how long a repair will take
It is the average length of past failures
It is a limit that must not be passed
It is a goal that the IT team sets for itself
options_why: A forecast tells what we expect. A limit tells what we refuse to go beyond.
The MTD is not a history. It is a limit for the future.
The owner defines it, not the IT team.
cards.answer: It is a limit that must not be passed
cards.explanation: A limit says what we refuse to go beyond. The MTD is a limit.

cards.question: Say in your own words what the MTD is.
cards.answer: The longest time a key function can stay stopped. After that, the harm lasts and the company is in danger.
cards.explanation: Think of your friends: after a long wait, they leave for good.

cards.question: Which statement about the MTD is NOT true?
options: The technicians who do the repair set it
The system owner sets it
Going past it means a risk that is too high
It is also called MAO
options_why: This is true. The manual says that the system owner defines it.
This is true. Exceeding the MTD is an unacceptable risk.
This is true. MAO means maximum acceptable outage.
cards.answer: The technicians who do the repair set it
cards.explanation: The system owner sets the MTD, because the owner is responsible for the function.

cards.question: The MTD of a function is passed. What does this mean for the business owner?
options: A normal event that the plan expects
A risk that is too high for the owner
A sign that the backups worked well
A risk that only the IT team must handle
options_why: The plan aims to stay under the MTD. Passing it is not normal.
Backups are about data. They do not measure the MTD.
The owner answers for the function, so the risk is the owner's.
cards.answer: A risk that is too high for the owner
cards.explanation: The manual says that exceeding the MTD is an expression of unacceptable risk by the business owner.

cards.question: A company never asks its owners how long each function can stop. Which risk is MOST likely?
options: Its recovery times will fit the business perfectly, by luck
Its backups will stop working
Its owners will no longer own the functions
Its recovery times may not fit the business
options_why: Without the limit, nobody knows what time is acceptable.
Backups do not depend on this question.
The owners stay the owners. The company just lacks information.
cards.answer: Its recovery times may not fit the business
cards.explanation: Without the MTD, the company cannot set a recovery time that fits the business.

cards.question: Who sets the MTD, and why?
cards.answer: The system owner. The owner answers for the function, so the owner knows what a long stop would cost.
cards.explanation: The limit comes from the business, not from the technology.

cards.question: Which question does the MTD answer?
options: How long can the function stop before lasting harm occurs?
How much data can we accept to lose after a failure?
How long will this repair take for the IT team?
Who caused this failure and who must pay for it?
options_why: That question is about data loss, not about time stopped.
That question is about the repair, not about the limit.
The cause is useful later. The MTD is about the limit.
cards.answer: How long can the function stop before lasting harm occurs?
cards.explanation: The MTD is the longest stop that the business can bear.

cards.question: What happens when the MTD is passed?
cards.answer: The harm becomes lasting and the survival of the company is at risk. The owner faces a risk that is too high.
cards.explanation: The MTD is the last border before lasting harm.

paragraphes: Your console crashed. You turn it on again and restart the game. It takes you six minutes.
Your friends ask: when will you be back? You say: ten minutes at most.
This promise is like the recovery time objective (RTO). It is the time that a company plans to need to restart.

decouverte.comme: You do not promise a time that makes your friends leave. You promise a shorter time, to stay well under their patience.
decouverte.enVrai: The RTO is the time that the company plans to need to get a function running again. It must be shorter than the MTD, or equal to it. If the RTO is too long, the company adds controls (extra protections) to make it shorter.

decouverte.question: How does the RTO of a function compare with its MTD?
options: Shorter than or equal to the MTD
Longer than the MTD
They have nothing to do with each other
decouverte.answer: Shorter than or equal to the MTD
decouverte.explanation: If the restart took longer than the limit, the harm would already be done. The other answers forget this link.

decouverte.texte: An online shop has an MTD of 24 hours. Its team sets an RTO of 4 hours. Within four hours, the site must take orders again. This keeps a big gap before the point of no return. These numbers are invented.

cards.question: Official definition: “recovery time objective (RTO)”
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the time that a company plans to need to make a system usable again, at a basic level.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “recovery time objective (RTO)”?
options: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the full service expectations of the system owner.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the customers.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to back up a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
options_why: The RTO aims at the minimum level of service. It does not aim at full service.
The sentence says that the system owner is the one who expects the service.
A backup is a copy of data. The RTO is about restoring the system.
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: planned time, restore a system, minimum service expectations, system owner.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “recovery time objective (RTO)” from memory.
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: Remember: planned time, restore, minimum service expectations.

cards.question: Official definition: “the link between RTO and MTD”
cards.answer: Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the restart time must end before the limit of harm. It can be shorter, or at most equal.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “the link between RTO and MTD”?
options: Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be more than or equal to the MTD.
Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be exactly equal to the MTD.
Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the RTO is exceeded, the MTD, by definition, must be less than or equal to the RTO.
Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be less than or equal to the MTD.
options_why: A restart longer than the MTD would come too late.
The RTO can be shorter than the MTD. It does not have to be exactly equal.
The two terms are swapped. The MTD is the limit, and the RTO must stay under it.
cards.answer: Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the MTD is exceeded, by definition, less than or equal to the MTD.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “the link between RTO and MTD” from memory.
cards.answer: Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: Three parts: unacceptable disaster, the MTD is exceeded, so the RTO is less than or equal to the MTD.

cards.question: Official definition: “the RTO as a maximum”
cards.answer: In other words, RTO is the maximum period of time within which a CBF must be restored after a disruption to avoid unacceptable business consequences.
cards.explanation: In simple words: it is the longest wait allowed before the function must work again.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “the RTO as a maximum” from memory.
cards.answer: In other words, RTO is the maximum period of time within which a CBF must be restored after a disruption to avoid unacceptable business consequences.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the maximum period of time, restored after a disruption, to avoid unacceptable business consequences.

cards.question: What does the RTO show?
options: The longest time a function can stay stopped before lasting harm
The planned time to get a system working again
The time between two backups
The money lost in one hour of downtime
options_why: That is the MTD, the limit. The RTO is the plan to stay under it.
Backups are about data, not about the time to restart.
Money lost is a cost. The RTO is a length of time.
cards.answer: The planned time to get a system working again
cards.explanation: The RTO is the time that the company plans to need to restart a system.

cards.question: The MTD of a function is ten hours. Which RTO follows the rule of the manual?
options: An RTO of twelve hours or less
An RTO of more than ten hours
An RTO of ten hours or less
Any RTO, because they are not linked
options_why: Twelve hours is past the limit of ten hours.
More than ten hours is past the limit.
They are linked. The RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.answer: An RTO of ten hours or less
cards.explanation: The RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.

cards.question: Which statement is correct?
options: The MTD is the limit, and the RTO stays under it
The RTO is the limit, and the MTD stays under it
The MTD and the RTO are always exactly the same number
The RTO is set by the vendor, and the MTD by the IT team
options_why: The two roles are swapped.
They are linked, but the RTO is usually shorter than the MTD.
The owner defines the MTD. The vendor does not set the RTO.
cards.answer: The MTD is the limit, and the RTO stays under it
cards.explanation: The limit is the MTD. The RTO is the time we plan, and it stays under the limit.

cards.question: What does RTO stand for?
cards.answer: Recovery time objective: the planned time to bring a system back to the minimum level of service.
cards.explanation: Time is in the name: the RTO is about the length of time to restart.

cards.question: A company plans six hours to restart its cash register system. Its MTD is four hours. What is the BEST action?
options: Keep the plan, because six hours is close enough
Add controls to bring the RTO under the four-hour MTD
Move the MTD to six hours so that it fits
Make one extra backup and keep the same plan
options_why: Almost is not enough. The RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.
The limit comes from what the business can bear. We do not move it to fit the plan.
An extra backup does not always make the restart faster.
cards.answer: Add controls to bring the RTO under the four-hour MTD
cards.explanation: The manual says that the RTO is adjusted with additional controls to bring it within the MTD.

cards.question: The RTO of a function is longer than its MTD. What should the company do FIRST?
options: Raise the MTD to match the RTO
Ask the owner to accept the risk
Ignore it, because the RTO is only a guess
Look for controls to shorten the recovery time
options_why: The limit does not change just because the plan is slow.
Accepting the risk comes only after the owner refuses to add controls.
The RTO is a plan. A plan that is too slow must be fixed.
cards.answer: Look for controls to shorten the recovery time
cards.explanation: First we try to bring the RTO within the MTD. Accepting the risk is the last choice.

cards.question: An owner will not pay for more controls. The RTO stays longer than the MTD. What is MOST accurate?
options: The owner accepted this risk
The RTO is now equal to the MTD by law
The MTD has moved by itself
The company now has no risk
options_why: No law makes the two numbers equal.
The limit does not move by itself.
The risk is still there. The owner has chosen to live with it.
cards.answer: The owner accepted this risk
cards.explanation: The manual says that at this point the owner has accepted the risk of operation.

cards.question: Say the rule that links the RTO and the MTD.
cards.answer: The RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: The RTO is the plan. The MTD is the limit.

cards.question: Which statement about the RTO is NOT true?
options: It is a planned time
It must be less than or equal to the MTD
It can be longer than the MTD
It is about reaching the minimum level of service
options_why: This is true. The RTO is planned in advance.
This is true. It is the rule of the manual.
This is true. The goal is the minimum service the owner expects.
cards.answer: It can be longer than the MTD
cards.explanation: By definition, the RTO is less than or equal to the MTD. It can never be longer.

cards.question: Which order is correct on the timeline after an incident?
options: Incident, then the end of the MTD, then the end of the RTO
End of the MTD, then incident, then end of the RTO
End of the RTO, then incident, then end of the MTD
Incident, then end of the RTO, then end of the MTD
options_why: The RTO must end before the MTD, not after it.
The incident starts the clocks. Nothing ends before it.
The RTO is counted after the incident, not before it.
cards.answer: Incident, then end of the RTO, then end of the MTD
cards.explanation: The system should work again (RTO) before the limit of lasting harm (MTD).

cards.question: A hospital has an MTD of two hours for its patient records. Which RTO is consistent?
options: Two hours and thirty minutes
One hour and thirty minutes
Three hours
Four hours
options_why: This is longer than the MTD of two hours.
This is longer than the MTD of two hours.
This is much longer than the MTD of two hours.
cards.answer: One hour and thirty minutes
cards.explanation: Only an RTO of two hours or less stays within the MTD.

cards.question: What can a company do if its RTO is longer than its MTD?
cards.answer: Add controls to make the recovery shorter. If the owner will not add controls, the owner accepts the risk.
cards.explanation: Each control costs money, so the choice belongs to the business owner.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: the RTO is adjusted by the application of additional controls.

cards.question: Why must the RTO be less than or equal to the MTD? Which reason is BEST?
options: The RTO is a cost of recovery and the MTD is a yearly budget
Technicians cannot work faster than the MTD
Harm lasts after the MTD, so recovery must end before
Customers always forgive a delay up to the MTD
options_why: These are not the meanings of the two terms. Both are lengths of time.
The MTD is a business limit. It says nothing about the speed of technicians.
The MTD is the point where harm becomes lasting. Customers may leave before it.
cards.answer: Harm lasts after the MTD, so recovery must end before
cards.explanation: If the recovery took longer than the MTD, the harm would already be done.

cards.question: Why can the RTO be set to a value much shorter than the MTD?
cards.answer: To keep a safe gap before the limit. A shorter RTO leaves room for surprises.
cards.explanation: A plan that ends right at the limit has no margin.

paragraphes: Your console crashes. You restart your game. Your game is there, but you lost the last ten minutes.
The game saves by itself every ten minutes. What you did after the last save is gone.
How many minutes of play can you accept to lose? In a company, this limit is the recovery point objective (RPO).

decouverte.titre: The more you save, the less you lose
decouverte.comme: If the game saves every minute, you lose little when the console crashes. But the console has to work much harder.
decouverte.enVrai: The RPO shows how much data the company accepts to lose, as a length of time. An RPO of one hour means: we can lose at most the last hour of work. The shorter the RPO, the more often we must back up. A backup is a copy of data. The image stops here: a company loses orders or payments, not only minutes of play.

decouverte.question: A shop saves its orders every 24 hours. It fails at 6 pm. What can it lose at worst?
options: The orders of the last day
Only the last minute
Nothing, because everything is already saved
decouverte.answer: The orders of the last day
decouverte.explanation: Everything that came in since the last backup is lost. The less often we back up, the bigger the possible loss.

decouverte.texte: A bank cannot lose a single payment, so its RPO is almost zero. An online bookshop can accept to lose one hour of orders, so its RPO is one hour. Each company chooses according to what it cannot afford to lose.

cards.question: Official definition: “recovery point objective (RPO)”
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: In simple words: how much data the company accepts to lose, shown as a length of time. Think of the minutes of play you lose after a crash.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “recovery point objective (RPO)”?
options: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable system downtime, represented as a period of time.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of expected data loss, represented as a period of time.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a number of files.
options_why: System downtime is the world of the MTD. The RPO is about data loss.
Tolerable means the loss that the business accepts. Expected is a forecast.
The RPO is shown as a length of time, not as a number of files.
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: measurement, tolerable data loss, period of time.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “recovery point objective (RPO)” from memory.
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: Three key words: measurement, tolerable data loss, period of time.

cards.question: Official definition: “who defines the RPO”
cards.answer: As with the MTD, this must be defined by the business, and the business is responsible for resourcing the controls to achieve the RPO.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the business decides how much loss is bearable, and the business pays for the controls that reach it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Resourcing means providing the means.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “who defines the RPO” from memory.
cards.answer: As with the MTD, this must be defined by the business, and the business is responsible for resourcing the controls to achieve the RPO.
cards.explanation: Three parts: defined by the business, responsible for resourcing the controls, to achieve the RPO.

cards.question: What does the RPO show?
options: How long the company can stay stopped without lasting harm
How much data the company accepts to lose
How long a restart will take after a failure
How many backups the company owns in total
options_why: That is the MTD, the limit of the stop.
That is the RTO, the planned restart time.
The number of backups is not the measure. The RPO is the loss that is accepted.
cards.answer: How much data the company accepts to lose
cards.explanation: The RPO is about data loss, shown as a time: for example, the last hour of work.

cards.question: A company accepts to lose at most one hour of data. How often must it back up, at the very least?
options: Once a day, at night
Once a week, on Friday
Once a month, at month end
At least every hour
options_why: With one backup a day, we can lose up to twenty-four hours of data.
With one backup a week, the loss can be a whole week.
With one backup a month, the loss can be a whole month.
cards.answer: At least every hour
cards.explanation: The maximum loss is the time since the last backup. So we back up at least as often as the RPO.

cards.question: Which measure looks backward in time, to the last backup?
options: The RPO, the data lost
The RTO, the time to restart
The MTD, the longest stop
The BIA, the study of the impact
options_why: The RTO looks forward, to the restart.
The MTD looks forward, to the limit of harm.
A BIA is a study. It is not a duration.
cards.answer: The RPO, the data lost
cards.explanation: The RPO looks backward. The RTO and the MTD look forward.

cards.question: What does RPO stand for?
cards.answer: Recovery point objective: the tolerable data loss, shown as a length of time.
cards.explanation: The point is the moment of the last backup, where we go back to.

cards.question: An online bookshop has an RPO of two hours. Its last backup is three hours old. What is the BEST conclusion?
options: It respects its RPO, because three hours is close
It must restart faster, because its RTO is too long
It breaks its RPO and must back up more often than it does now
It must raise its MTD to three hours
options_why: The gap is bigger than two hours. Close is not enough.
The restart time is not the problem here. The age of the backup is.
The MTD is a different limit. Moving it does not fix the data loss.
cards.answer: It breaks its RPO and must back up more often than it does now
cards.explanation: The gap since the last backup is bigger than the RPO. The shop risks losing more data than it accepts.

cards.question: Which company MOST needs an RPO close to zero?
options: A blog that shares old photos
A school that posts its menu once a week
A shop that prints a newsletter each month
A bank that records payments
options_why: Old photos are already saved. A short loss would not hurt much.
A menu can be written again in a few minutes.
A newsletter can be rebuilt without much harm.
cards.answer: A bank that records payments
cards.explanation: A bank cannot lose a single payment, so it needs a very short RPO.

cards.question: A company has no RPO. What should it do FIRST?
options: Buy the fastest backup system on the market
Ask the business how much loss it accepts
Let the IT team choose the shortest RPO possible
Copy the RPO of a large competitor
options_why: We should not buy a tool before we know the need.
The shortest RPO costs a lot. The business must decide if it is worth it.
Another company has other data and other needs.
cards.answer: Ask the business how much loss it accepts
cards.explanation: The business defines the RPO. The technicians then provide the means.

cards.question: How is the RPO linked to how often we back up?
cards.answer: We must back up at least as often as the RPO. An RPO of one hour needs a backup every hour or faster.
cards.explanation: The gap between two backups is the worst loss.

cards.question: Who is BEST placed to define the RPO?
options: The technicians who run the backup system
The vendor who sold the backup tool
The people who run the business
An outside auditor who checks the business
options_why: Technicians provide the means, but the business knows what it can lose.
A vendor wants to sell tools. It does not know the business.
An auditor checks the work. The auditor does not define it.
cards.answer: The people who run the business
cards.explanation: As with the MTD, the RPO is defined by the business.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a result of a very short RPO?
options: Less storage and less network use for backups
More frequent backups during the day
A higher cost for the company
More work for the IT team every week
options_why: A short RPO means backing up very often.
More backups cost more money.
More backups mean more work.
cards.answer: Less storage and less network use for backups
cards.explanation: A very short RPO needs more backups, so it needs more storage, more network use, and more work.

cards.question: A shop backs up its orders once every 24 hours. It fails at 6 pm. What can it lose at worst?
options: Only the last minute of orders
The orders of the last 24 hours
Only the orders made after the failure
Nothing, because the backup is complete
options_why: The loss is everything since the last backup, not only a minute.
Orders made after the failure are another problem. The backup cannot save them.
A backup that is a day old does not hold today's orders.
cards.answer: The orders of the last 24 hours
cards.explanation: Everything that came in since the last backup is lost. The less often we back up, the bigger the loss.

cards.question: Why does a very short RPO cost more?
cards.answer: We must back up very often. This needs more storage, more network use, and more work.
cards.explanation: Every extra backup uses resources.

cards.question: Which statement is MOST correct?
options: A short RTO always means a short RPO
The RPO is counted after the incident, like the RTO
The RPO and the RTO are two names for one thing
A company can restart fast and still lose a lot of data
options_why: The two are separate. A fast restart does not mean few lost data.
The RPO is counted before the incident, back to the last backup.
They measure different things: data lost and time to restart.
cards.answer: A company can restart fast and still lose a lot of data
cards.explanation: The RPO and the RTO are two separate choices.

cards.question: Who must pay for the controls that reach the RPO?
cards.answer: The business. It defines the RPO, and it is responsible for resourcing the controls.
cards.explanation: An RPO without the means to reach it makes no sense.

paragraphes: Your console crashes. You think of three things, and each one has its own clock.
When was I last saved? How long will I need to restart? How long will my friends wait for me?
In a company, these clocks are the RPO, the RTO, and the MTD. People often mix them up.

decouverte.comme: You draw a line. In the middle is the crash. On the left, the time since the last save. On the right, the time to restart, and then the moment when your friends leave for good.
decouverte.enVrai: To the left of the incident is the RPO: how far back we lose data. To the right are the RTO, the time to restart, and the MTD, the limit of lasting harm. The RPO looks backward. The RTO and the MTD look forward.

decouverte.question: A failure happens at noon. The last backup is from nine o'clock. Which measure do these three hours show?
options: The RPO: the data loss
The RTO: the time to restart
The MTD: the survival limit
decouverte.explanation: These three hours are the data lost since the last backup. The RTO and the MTD are counted after the failure.

decouverte.texte: An online pharmacy backs up its orders every hour, so its RPO is one hour. It wants to restart within two hours, so its RTO is two hours. After twelve hours of downtime, too many customers go elsewhere, so its MTD is twelve hours. These choices depend on its risk tolerance, which is the amount of danger it accepts to face. The numbers are invented.

cards.question: Official definition: “MTD, RTO and RPO”
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
cards.explanation: In simple words: these three limits are the key numbers for planning. They say how long the company can wait and how much it can lose.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word. A threshold is a limit.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “MTD, RTO and RPO”?
options: MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
MTD, RTO, and RPO are optional thresholds for business continuity planning.
MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for security awareness training.
MTD, RTO, and BIA are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
options_why: The sentence says essential. These thresholds are not optional.
The thresholds are used to plan continuity, not to plan training.
A BIA is a study, not a threshold. The three thresholds are MTD, RTO, and RPO.
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: MTD, RTO, and RPO, essential thresholds, business continuity planning.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “MTD, RTO and RPO” from memory.
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
cards.explanation: Three parts: MTD, RTO, and RPO; essential thresholds; business continuity planning.

cards.question: Official definition: “MTD, RTO and RPO and risk”
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are important planning horizons and estimates that are strongly linked to an organization's risk tolerance.
cards.explanation: In simple words: these durations depend on the amount of danger that the company accepts to face.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note after figure 1.4. A planning horizon is how far ahead you plan.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “MTD, RTO and RPO and risk” from memory.
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are important planning horizons and estimates that are strongly linked to an organization's risk tolerance.
cards.explanation: Three parts: important planning horizons, strongly linked, to the risk tolerance.

cards.question: How far back did we lose data? Which measure answers this question?
options: The RTO, the restart time
The MTD, the survival limit
The RPO, the data loss
The BIA, the impact study
options_why: The RTO is about the time to restart.
The MTD is about the longest stop.
A BIA is a study of the impact. It is not a time.
cards.answer: The RPO, the data loss
cards.explanation: The RPO looks backward to the last backup.

cards.question: How long will it take to restart the system? Which measure answers this question?
options: The RPO, the data loss
The MTD, the survival limit
The BCP, the written plan
The RTO, the restart time
options_why: The RPO is about lost data.
The MTD is the limit, not the planned time.
The BCP is a plan, not a measure.
cards.answer: The RTO, the restart time
cards.explanation: The RTO is the planned time to start again.

cards.question: How long can the function stay stopped before lasting harm? Which measure answers?
options: The RPO, the data loss
The MTD, the survival limit
The RTO, the restart time
The CBF, a key business function
options_why: The RPO is about lost data.
The RTO is the plan to stay under the limit.
A CBF is a key function, not a duration.
cards.answer: The MTD, the survival limit
cards.explanation: The MTD is the longest stop that the business can bear.

cards.question: Which measure is about data loss?
cards.answer: The RPO. It looks backward to the last backup.
cards.explanation: RPO is before the incident.

cards.question: A system fails at noon. The last backup was made at nine. What do these three hours show?
options: The restart time, which is compared with the RTO
The survival limit, which is compared with the MTD
The data loss, which is compared with the planned RPO
The time to warn the staff
options_why: Restart time is counted after the failure, not before it.
The survival limit is counted after the failure too.
Warning the staff is not the topic of these three hours.
cards.answer: The data loss, which is compared with the planned RPO
cards.explanation: The time since the last backup is the data that is lost.

cards.question: A company loses 3 hours of data and takes 5 hours to restart. Its MTD is 4 hours. Which statement is BEST?
options: The restart of 5 hours is past the MTD of 4 hours by one hour
The data loss of 3 hours goes past the MTD
The 3 and 5 hours add up, so only the total matters
All is fine, because 3 hours is less than 4 hours
options_why: Data loss is compared with the RPO, not with the MTD.
The data loss is another counter. We do not add it to the downtime.
The downtime counts. Five hours is longer than four.
cards.answer: The restart of 5 hours is past the MTD of 4 hours by one hour
cards.explanation: The restart time (RTO) must stay under the limit (MTD). Here five hours is more than four.

cards.question: Which order is correct on the timeline, from left to right?
options: Incident, last backup, system restarted, and then serious harm
Last backup, incident, system restarted, serious harm
Last backup, incident, serious harm, system restarted
System restarted, last backup, incident, serious harm
options_why: The last backup is made before the incident.
The system should restart before the harm becomes serious.
The restart cannot come before the incident.
cards.answer: Last backup, incident, system restarted, serious harm
cards.explanation: The data loss is before the incident. The restart comes after it, before the limit of harm.

cards.question: Which two measures are counted after the incident?
cards.answer: The RTO and the MTD. They look forward from the incident.
cards.explanation: The RTO is the plan. The MTD is the limit.

cards.question: Which statement about time is MOST correct?
options: The RTO looks backward, and the RPO and the MTD look forward
The MTD looks backward, and the RPO and the RTO look forward
All three measures look forward
The RPO looks backward, and the RTO and MTD look forward
options_why: The roles are swapped.
The MTD is a limit after the incident, not before it.
The RPO is about data lost before the incident.
cards.answer: The RPO looks backward, and the RTO and MTD look forward
cards.explanation: RPO is before the incident. RTO and MTD are after it.

cards.question: Which statement about MTD, RTO, and RPO is NOT true?
options: They are strict walls in a real crisis
They are essential thresholds for planning
They are strongly linked to risk tolerance
Leaders can adapt them in real time
options_why: This is true. The manual calls them essential thresholds.
This is true. They depend on the danger that a company accepts.
This is true. In a real event, leaders usually adapt them.
cards.answer: They are strict walls in a real crisis
cards.explanation: The manual says that they are more like guidelines than strict survival limits.

cards.question: A company sets an MTD but forgets to set an RTO. What is the MOST likely problem?
options: Nobody knows how much data can be lost
Nobody knows how long the function can stay stopped
Nobody knows how fast the system must restart after a failure
Nobody will need backups any more
options_why: That is the question of the RPO. It was not forgotten here.
That is the MTD. The company has already set it.
Backups are still needed. They do not depend on the RTO.
cards.answer: Nobody knows how fast the system must restart after a failure
cards.explanation: The MTD says where the wall is. The RTO says how fast to run to stay away from it.

cards.question: In a real crisis, are the three thresholds strict walls?
cards.answer: Not always. Leaders adapt on the spot, so they are more like guides than strict survival limits.
cards.explanation: They are mostly used to plan before the crisis.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note after figure 1.4.

cards.question: A bank says: we cannot lose any payment. Which measure is it describing?
options: A very short restart time (RTO)
A very long MTD
A very long RTO
A very short RPO
options_why: The RTO is about the time to restart, not about lost data.
The MTD is about the stop, not about lost data.
The RTO is about the time to restart, not about lost data.
cards.answer: A very short RPO
cards.explanation: Losing nothing means a very short RPO, close to zero.

cards.question: What do MTD, RTO, and RPO depend on?
cards.answer: The risk tolerance of the organization: the amount of danger that it accepts to face.
cards.explanation: A company that accepts more risk may choose longer times.

concepts.name: The continuity plan: scope and people

paragraphes: At school, there is a fire drill. Before you save any computer or notebook, one thing matters: everybody gets out.
Then the school plans where to meet, who calls the parents, and how to restart the lessons.
A continuity plan works the same way. People come first, then ways of working, then tools. The manual says: people, processes, technologies.

decouverte.comme: First we count the students. Then we plan how lessons restart. The computers come last.
decouverte.enVrai: In a business continuity plan (BCP), the order is fixed: people, then processes (ways of working), then technologies (tools and systems). A machine can be replaced, but a person cannot. The image stops here: all three are needed. The order only says what to protect first.

decouverte.question: A fire hits the offices of a company. What does the continuity plan protect first of all?
options: The people
The backups
The customers' orders
decouverte.explanation: Backups and orders matter, but the first goal of the plan is the safety of people.

decouverte.titre: The plan of a chain of stores
decouverte.texte: A chain of stores has shops in many cities and countries. Its plan must cover all of them. It lists the key functions, the threats, and the weak points. It also plans data backups, the people in the plan, communication, and tests.

cards.question: Official definition: “the order of a BCP”
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a continuity plan deals with people first, then ways of working, then technology.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “the order of a BCP”?
options: As with any good plan, a BCP involves technologies, processes, and people — in that order.
As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, technologies, and processes — in that order.
As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in any order.
options_why: The order is reversed. People come first.
Processes come before technologies in the real sentence.
The order matters. It says what to protect first.
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: people, processes, and technologies, in that order.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “the order of a BCP” from memory.
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: The three words in order: people, processes, technologies.

cards.question: Official definition: “the first goal of a BCP”
cards.answer: The first goal of any BCP must be to ensure the safety of your people during and after an emergency.
cards.explanation: In simple words: before the data and the machines, the first goal is the safety of people.
